title: Nirmal Purja Confirmed Dead After Broad Peak Avalanche Kills All 10 Climbers
excerpt: The record-breaking Nepali-British mountaineer, famed for climbing all 14 eight-thousanders in six months, was among 10 climbers caught in a midday avalanche on Pakistan's 12th-highest peak.
body:
• Nirmal "Nimsdai" Purja, 43, confirmed dead by his company Elite Exped after a Thursday avalanche on Broad Peak in Pakistan
  • All 10 climbers on the expedition are believed dead; three bodies recovered so far from the 8,051-metre peak
  • The Nepali-British mountaineer held the record for fastest ascent of all 14 eight-thousanders, completed in six months in 2019
  • Recovery of remaining bodies hampered by avalanche-prone terrain and Pakistan's limited high-altitude helicopter rescue capacity

Record-Breaking Climber Falls on Pakistan's Broad Peak

Nirmal "Nimsdai" Purja, the Nepali-British mountaineer who rose to global fame for climbing all 14 of the world's peaks above 8,000 metres in just over six months, has been confirmed dead following an avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak.

https://x.com/PopBase/status/2083563802176446595

"Today it is with profound sadness and immense heartbreak that we confirm that Nirmal 'Nimsdai' Purja tragically lost his life following the avalanche on Broad Peak," his expedition company Elite Exped said in an Instagram post on Saturday.

"Today, we mourn not only Nims, but every life lost in this tragedy including his trusted climbing partners and guides."

— Nimsdai Foundation, Instagram statement

Ten Climbers Caught in Midday Avalanche

Purja, 43, was among 10 mountaineers struck by an avalanche around midday on Thursday while ascending between Camp 2 and Camp 3 at approximately 6,600 metres on the 8,051-metre (26,414-foot) peak, the world's 12th-highest mountain in Pakistan's Gilgit-Baltistan region.

Search crews recovered three bodies on Friday — US climber Sarah Mallory Geis, Omani mountaineer Nadhira Al Harthy, and Nepali guide Pur Bahadur Gurung. The remaining bodies, including Purja's, were spotted and identified via drone footage but have not yet been retrieved.

"They are in a difficult spot and have not been retrieved yet," Chhang Dawa Sherpa, a board director of Seven Summit Treks, told Reuters. He noted that unlike Nepal, Pakistan does not have the practice of long-line helicopter rescue on mountains.

A Life of Extraordinary Achievement

Born in Nepal and later a British citizen, Purja served in the British military with the Gurkhas and subsequently in the Special Boat Service. In 2019, he completed the fastest-ever ascent of all 14 eight-thousanders — peaks exceeding 8,000 metres — in just six months and six days, shattering the previous record of nearly eight years.

His feat was chronicled in the 2021 Netflix documentary 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible, which brought him international recognition beyond the mountaineering community. He co-owned Elite Exped and had founded the Nimsdai Foundation in 2022.

"He made the impossible happen."

— Naila Kiani, Pakistan Alpine Club spokesperson

Recovery Efforts Continue Under Dangerous Conditions

Emergency workers have expressed concerns about the prospect of further avalanches hampering the recovery operation. Naila Kiani, a spokesperson for the Pakistan Alpine Club who previously climbed with Purja, warned that the remaining climbers' chances of survival "are very slim now."

"Pakistani mountains are very different to Nepal. Some of those areas are still avalanche prone, so our rescue team has to be very careful to assess whether they are endangering their lives," she told the BBC.

The six other climbers on the expedition included Pakistani climber Sohail Sakhi from Hunza, Chinese climber Wang Zong, and Nepali guides Nima Sherpa, Gyalu Sherpa, Nwang Thendou Sherpa, and Kili Pemba Sherpa. Elite Exped confirmed that other expedition members "sadly did not survive" without providing further details.

Diaspora Mourns a Pioneer

The tragedy has reverberated through South Asian mountaineering and diaspora communities worldwide. Purja had spoken of wanting to use his platform to honour Sherpa climbers. "Even though they were top climbers, they didn't get the right recognition," he told CNN in 2019. "Hopefully, I thought I could uplift their names."

Among the dead, Al Harthy had used her profile to empower Muslim women and girls in endurance sports, while Geis was known in American climbing circles. The disaster marks one of the deadliest incidents on Broad Peak in recent memory.
